traits: Round, coin-shaped leaves with the stalk attached at the center of the underside, like a tiny umbrella or lily pad
Scalloped (slightly toothed) leaf edges
Low, spreading growth that thickens fast in soggy or overwatered turf
White rhizomes just under the surface connect the leaves in a spreading patch

look_alikes.difference: Dollarweed has round leaves on individual stalks; matchweed has small toothed oval leaves in opposite pairs and a purple-and-white "match head" flower.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of a single leaf from above, showing whether it is round with a center-attached stalk or oval with opposite pairs along a stem.

copy.what_it_means: A round-leafed weed that thrives wherever soil stays wet, so a thick patch usually signals overwatering, a leaky irrigation zone, or poor drainage rather than a lawn problem on its own. A technician looks at the weed, turf type, season, and coverage, since the wet spot behind it needs addressing too.
copy.fact: Its round leaves attach to the stalk right at the center of the underside, like a tiny umbrella, which is where its lily-pad look comes from.
copy.blurb: A round-leafed weed that signals wet soil — check the sprinkler zone and drainage along with treating it.

tech_notes: Confirm irrigation schedule and drainage at the site before treatment; white rhizomes must be fully removed by hand-pulling or the patch regrows. Per label if herbicide is used.

review.notes: Owner re-approved 2026-10-02 after the UF/IFAS season check of the yard calendar.

id_cues: Round, coin-sized leaves with the stalk attached dead-center on the underside
Scalloped leaf edge, visible on close inspection
Dig at the base — thin white rhizomes connect nearby plants just under the soil
Shows up first in the wettest or most overwatered part of the lawn

traits: Rough, hairy stems and thick, hairy, opposite leaves that feel sandpapery
Small white, star-shaped flowers clustered at the stem tips
Low, prostrate mat that spreads outward from a central point
Forms dense patches quickly once it flowers and sets seed

look_alikes.difference: Florida pusley has hairy stems and leaves with white star-shaped flowers; spotted spurge has smooth leaves with a maroon spot and oozes milky sap when broken.
look_alikes.next_photo: Wearing gloves, a close-up of a broken stem (milky sap or not) and the leaf surface (hairy vs. smooth with a center spot); keep any sap away from your eyes.

look_alikes.difference: Florida pusley has hairy stems, clustered white flowers; matchweed has smooth toothed leaves and one purple-and-white "match head" flower on a bare stalk.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the flower head (loose star-shaped cluster vs. one round match-head bloom on a bare stalk).

copy.what_it_means: A common summer weed in thin or newly established turf that spreads fast once it flowers, since each plant produces abundant seed. A technician looks at how thin the turf is where it's showing up, along with the season and coverage, before recommending an approach.
copy.fact: Its small white flowers can turn a thin patch of lawn into a solid stand of pusley within a few weeks, since a single plant produces an abundance of seed.
copy.blurb: A fast-seeding summer weed that fills in wherever the turf is thin.

tech_notes: Sometimes cited as a possible indicator of plant-parasitic nematode pressure on the turf underneath; note but do not diagnose nematodes from the weed alone. Hand-digging removes the taproot; herbicide per label if used.

id_cues: Stems and leaves feel rough and hairy to the touch
Small white star-shaped flowers cluster at the tips of the stems
Grows low and prostrate, forming a thickening mat
Leaves are thick, fleshy, and grow in opposite pairs

traits: Small, oblong leaves in opposite pairs, each with an irregular maroon-to-purple spot in the center
Breaking a stem oozes a milky white sap
Low, flat, mat-forming growth that hugs the ground and does not root at the nodes
Shows up first in dry, thin, or sandy patches of turf, sidewalk cracks, and beds

look_alikes.difference: Spotted spurge has smooth leaves with a maroon spot and milky sap when broken; Florida pusley has hairy stems, no sap, and clustered white star-shaped flowers.
look_alikes.next_photo: Wearing gloves, a close-up of a broken stem (milky sap or not) and the leaf surface (spotted and smooth vs. hairy); keep any sap away from your eyes.

look_alikes.difference: Spotted spurge has a maroon leaf spot and oozes milky sap when broken; matchweed has plain green leaves, no sap, and a purple-and-white "match head" flower.
look_alikes.next_photo: Wearing gloves, a close-up of a broken stem and the leaf surface; keep any sap away from your eyes.

safety_line: Breaking a stem releases a milky sap that can irritate skin or eyes; wash it off and avoid touching your face after handling this weed.

copy.what_it_means: A low mat-forming weed that moves into thin, dry, or stressed turf and produces seed quickly once established. A technician looks at how thin the surrounding turf is, the season, and coverage before recommending an approach, since a thicker lawn is what keeps it from coming back.
copy.fact: Breaking a stem releases a milky white sap — a quick tell apart from look-alikes that don't ooze sap. Wear gloves, keep the sap away from your eyes, and wash off any that touches skin, since it can irritate.
copy.blurb: A ground-hugging weed with a milky sap and a spot on each leaf, thriving in thin or dry turf.

tech_notes: Present in both dry and overwatered thin turf; sometimes cited alongside pusley as a possible nematode indicator — do not diagnose nematodes from the weed alone. Per label if herbicide is used. Sap can irritate skin or eyes on contact; wash exposed skin.

id_cues: Small oblong leaves in opposite pairs, each with a maroon-to-purple center spot
Break a stem and check for milky white sap
Grows flat against the ground rather than rooting upward at the nodes
Common first in the driest, thinnest, or most compacted part of the lawn

traits: Small, rounded leaflets arranged in two flat rows along the branchlets, resembling a miniature mimosa tree
Tiny, warty, bead-like fruits lined up along the underside of each leaf branch
Grows upright from a taproot rather than sprawling flat
Base becomes woody as the plant matures, making it tougher to pull

look_alikes.difference: Chamberbitter has tiny bead-like fruits under the leaflets and doesn't fold when touched; sensitive plant folds at a touch and has pink powderpuff flowers.
look_alikes.next_photo: Gently touch a leaflet, avoiding the prickly stems, and photograph the reaction (folds vs. no reaction), plus a close-up of a leaf branch underside for beaded fruit.

copy.what_it_means: A warm-season weed that looks harmless as a seedling but is easiest to deal with early — once its base turns woody later in summer, it gets noticeably tougher to remove. A technician looks at how far along the plants are and how much of the lawn is affected before recommending an approach.
copy.fact: Its seed pods split open explosively when they mature, flinging seeds away from the parent plant, which is part of why a few missed plants can reseed a whole bed the next year.
copy.blurb: A mimosa look-alike weed that's easy to pull young and much tougher once its base turns woody.

tech_notes: Timing matters — pre-emergence or early post-emergence control is far more effective than waiting until the base has hardened. Per label if herbicide is used.

id_cues: Rows of small, rounded leaflets along flat branchlets, like a tiny mimosa
Tiny warty, bead-like fruits tucked along the underside of the leaf branch
Grows upright on a single stem from a taproot, not flat along the ground
Leaves do not fold or react when touched (unlike sensitive plant)

traits: Small oval leaves with toothed tips, arranged in opposite pairs on hairy, branching stems
Round flower head with a purple center ringed by tiny white blooms — the "match head" look
Long creeping stems (stolons) that root at the nodes and form dense mats
Low growth, usually under a foot tall, spreading several feet from one plant

look_alikes.difference: Matchweed has small opposite, toothed leaves and a round purple-and-white flower head; dollarweed has round leaves on individual stalks and no showy flower.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of a single leaf and whether a round "match head" flower is present on a stalk.

look_alikes.difference: Matchweed has smooth, toothed leaves and one round match-head flower per stalk; Florida pusley has hairy stems and a loose cluster of small white flowers.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the flower head (one round bloom vs. a loose cluster) and leaf surface (smooth vs. hairy).

look_alikes.difference: Matchweed has plain green leaves, no sap, and a round match-head flower; spotted spurge has a maroon leaf spot and oozes milky sap when a stem is broken.
look_alikes.next_photo: Wearing gloves, a close-up of a broken stem (sap or not) and the leaf surface (spotted vs. plain); keep any sap away from your eyes.

copy.what_it_means: A native, low-growing groundcover that some homeowners actually keep on purpose in low-traffic areas, and that shows up as a weed elsewhere in the lawn. It's mostly a cosmetic issue in turf a customer wants uniform, and a technician weighs the weed type, turf type, season, and coverage before suggesting anything.
copy.fact: Its round flower head, with a ring of tiny white blooms around a purple center, is where the name "matchweed" comes from — it looks like a struck match head on a stalk.
copy.blurb: A native groundcover weed with a distinctive purple-and-white "match head" bloom — mostly a cosmetic issue in a lawn.

tech_notes: Distinguish from an intentional groundcover planting before recommending removal; a pollinator-friendly native, so weigh customer preference before treating. Per label if herbicide is used.

id_cues: Round flower head with a purple center ringed by tiny white flowers, on a bare stalk
Small, opposite, oval leaves with toothed tips
Long creeping stems root at each node, forming a dense mat
Stems and leaves feel slightly hairy

traits: Opposite, lance-shaped leaves with no leaf stalk, joined across the stem by a thin membrane
Small white, tubular flowers with four petal lobes, star-shaped when viewed from the front
Hairy, branching stems that spread flat and root along the ground
Tolerates very low mowing heights, unlike most other broadleaf weeds

look_alikes.difference: Virginia buttonweed has lance-shaped opposite leaves and small white four-lobed flowers; dollarweed has round leaves on individual stalks with no showy flower.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of a single leaf (lance-shaped vs. round) and whether small white flowers are present along the stem.

look_alikes.difference: Virginia buttonweed has narrow lance-shaped leaves and small white flowers; doveweed has fleshy stems, sheathing leaf bases, and purple three-petaled flowers.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of a leaf blade shape and whether it looks grass-like (doveweed) or narrow and lance-shaped (buttonweed).

copy.what_it_means: A mat-forming weed that favors moist to wet turf and is genuinely persistent — a piece of stem or root left behind after pulling can start a new plant. A technician looks at the wet spot behind it as well as the weed itself, turf type, season, and coverage.
copy.fact: A broken stem or root fragment left in the soil can grow into a whole new plant, which is part of why hand-pulling alone so often leaves it looking like it came right back.
copy.blurb: A wet-soil weed that regrows from leftover stem or root fragments — persistent, but not aggressive turf-wide.

tech_notes: Address the underlying moisture/drainage issue alongside any treatment; regrowth from fragments is the main reason hand-pulling underperforms. Per label if herbicide is used; note it tolerates very low mowing heights.

id_cues: Opposite lance-shaped leaves with no stalk, joined at the stem by a thin membrane
Small white flowers with four petal lobes, star-shaped from the front
Hairy stems spread flat and root as they go
Still visible even in a very low-mowed lawn, unlike most broadleaf weeds

traits: Three heart-shaped leaflets per leaf, like a clover but each leaflet notched at the tip
Small, five-petaled yellow flowers
Slender, upright seed pods that look like tiny okra pods
Pods burst open when touched, flinging seeds several feet

look_alikes.difference: Yellow woodsorrel has heart-shaped leaflets and yellow flowers; common lespedeza has oblong leaflets with parallel veins and small pink-purple flowers.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the leaflet shape (heart-shaped vs. oblong) and the flower color (yellow vs. pink-purple).

look_alikes.difference: Yellow woodsorrel has heart-shaped leaflets, yellow flowers, exploding pods; creeping beggarweed has pointed leaflets, pink-purple flowers, sticky flat pods.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the leaflet shape and the seed pod (slender and upright vs. flat and segmented).

copy.what_it_means: A clover look-alike that pops up in beds and thin turf and spreads itself by flinging seed from its own pods when brushed or mowed. It's mostly a cosmetic nuisance in a lawn, and a technician looks at the weed type, turf type, season, and coverage before recommending an approach.
copy.fact: Its slender seed pods act like tiny spring-loaded cannons, launching seeds several feet away the moment they're bumped or brushed.
copy.blurb: A clover look-alike with yellow flowers and exploding seed pods that fling seed across the bed.

tech_notes: Often confused with clover by customers; confirm the notched, heart-shaped leaflet and yellow flower before treatment. Per label if herbicide is used.

id_cues: Three heart-shaped leaflets per leaf, each notched at the tip, like a clover
Small, five-petaled yellow flowers
Slender, upright seed pods resembling miniature okra
Touch a mature pod — it bursts and flings seed

traits: Smooth, narrow, opposite leaves on thin, branching, sprawling stems
Tiny white four-petaled flowers, usually two or more on long paired stalks
Low, spreading mat, rarely taller than about six inches
Common in moist lawns and garden beds

look_alikes.difference: Old world diamond-flower has thin stems, tiny white flowers on paired stalks; Virginia buttonweed is coarser, with hairy stems, larger flowers against the stem.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the flower stalk (long thin paired stalks vs. flowers sitting flush against a hairy stem).

look_alikes.difference: Old world diamond-flower has thin wiry stems with tiny white flowers; dayflower has thick, fleshy, succulent stems with broader leaves and showy blue flowers.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the stem thickness (thin and wiry vs. thick and fleshy) and the flower color.

copy.what_it_means: A fine, wiry annual weed that spreads across moist lawns and garden beds and is easy to overlook until it forms a mat. A technician looks at the weed type, turf type, season, and coverage before recommending an approach.
copy.fact: It's originally from Asia and Africa, and despite its delicate look it can quickly carpet a moist bed once established.
copy.blurb: A fine, wiry weed that fills moist lawns and beds — easy to miss until it forms a mat.

tech_notes: Confirm against buttonweed and dayflower before treatment; thin stems and tiny flowers are the distinguishing tell. Per label if herbicide is used.

review.notes: County-level SWFL prevalence (Sarasota/Charlotte/Manatee/Lee/Collier) is unconfirmed — the Atlas of Florida Plants distribution map is JS-rendered and did not yield county voucher text in this pass; life cycle is confirmed annual per UF/IFAS Mid-Florida REC.

id_cues: Thin, wiry, branching stems that sprawl low across the ground
Narrow, smooth, opposite leaves
Tiny white four-petaled flowers on long paired stalks
Common in lawns and beds that stay moist

traits: Flat rosette of lobed leaves low to the ground, easily mistaken for a small dandelion
Thin, upright, branching flower stalk rising well above the leaf rosette
Small clusters of yellow, dandelion-like flowers at the top of the stalk
Common in cool-season thin turf, beds, and disturbed soil

look_alikes.difference: Asiatic hawksbeard has a flat, lobed rosette and a tall stalk with small yellow flowers; cudweed has soft, fuzzy leaves and whitish-brown flowers instead.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the flower color (yellow vs. whitish-brown) and whether the leaves look soft/fuzzy or smooth and lobed.

copy.what_it_means: A cool-season weed that's often mistaken for a small dandelion and tends to move into thin turf over the winter months. A technician looks at how thin the turf is, the season, and coverage before recommending an approach.
copy.fact: It's frequently mistaken for dandelion, but its flower clusters are smaller and its leaf rosette sits flatter against the ground.
copy.blurb: A dandelion look-alike that moves into thin winter turf.

tech_notes: Cool-season annual — expect it to fade as warm-season turf resumes active growth in spring; thin turf is the underlying driver. Per label if herbicide is used.

id_cues: Flat rosette of lobed leaves low to the ground
Tall, thin, branching flower stalk well above the leaves
Small clusters of yellow, dandelion-like flowers at the top
Shows up in cool months in thin turf and disturbed soil

traits: Three leaflets per leaf, rounded at the base and tapering to a point, on hairy stems
Small pink-to-purple, pea-shaped flowers in summer
Flat, segmented seed pods that stick to clothing and pet fur
Grows prostrate in mowed turf but can stand upright in unmowed beds

look_alikes.difference: Creeping beggarweed leaflets round at the base, tapering to a point, with sticky pods; common lespedeza leaflets are oblong with parallel veins, a spur tip.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of a single leaflet shape and whether a flat, segmented seed pod is present.

look_alikes.difference: Creeping beggarweed has rounder, pointed leaflets, pink-purple flowers, sticky pods; yellow woodsorrel has heart-shaped leaflets, yellow flowers, bursting pods.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the leaflet shape and flower color.

copy.what_it_means: A perennial weed that favors full-sun, dry, thin turf and spreads its sticky seed pods on clothes, socks, and pet fur. A technician looks at how thin the turf is, the season, and coverage before recommending an approach.
copy.fact: Its flat, segmented seed pods are built to hitch a ride — they cling to fabric and fur, which is how it spreads from yard to yard.
copy.blurb: A perennial weed that thrives in thin, dry turf and hitches rides on clothes and pets via its sticky pods.

tech_notes: Favors dry, full-sun, thin turf rather than wet areas — distinguishes it from most other broadleaf weeds in this file. Per label if herbicide is used.

id_cues: Three leaflets per leaf, rounded at the base and tapering to a point
Small pink-to-purple pea-shaped flowers
Flat, segmented seed pods that stick to clothes and fur
Lies flat when mowed, but can stand upright in an unmowed bed

traits: Three oblong leaflets per leaf, with parallel side veins running nearly straight out to the smooth edge
A tiny spur at the tip of each leaflet
Small pink-to-purple flowers tucked into the leaf joints along the stem
Grows low, dense, and mat-like, close to the ground

look_alikes.difference: Common lespedeza leaflets are oblong, parallel veins, a spur tip; creeping beggarweed leaflets are rounder at the base, tapering to a point, with sticky pods.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the leaflet shape and vein pattern, and whether a flat segmented seed pod is present.

look_alikes.difference: Common lespedeza has oblong leaflets, small flowers tucked at leaf joints; yellow woodsorrel has heart-shaped leaflets, yellow flowers on own stalks.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the leaflet shape and flower color.

copy.what_it_means: A low mat-forming weed that shows up most in thin, dry, low-nutrient turf — especially centipedegrass lawns. Fixing the underlying thinness helps as much as anything; a technician evaluates turf and soil, and any nutrition correction stays within the local fertilizer rules.
copy.fact: It's closely tied to soils low in available nitrogen, which is part of why it shows up so often in centipedegrass lawns that are deliberately kept on a lean feeding schedule.
copy.blurb: A mat-forming weed that favors thin, low-nutrient turf, especially centipedegrass lawns.

tech_notes: Associated with low-nitrogen, thin turf (notably centipedegrass); grows close to the ground and mows poorly. A technician times any nutrition adjustment within the local fertilizer rules.

review.notes: No dedicated UF/IFAS EDIS publication for this species was found live; core ID facts (trifoliate leaflets, low-N/centipedegrass association, July–Oct flowering) are corroborated by a UF/IFAS Nassau County Extension post and Clemson HGIC rather than a core EDIS page.

id_cues: Three oblong leaflets with straight parallel side veins and a tiny spur at the tip
Small pink-to-purple flowers tucked in at the leaf joints
Grows low and mat-like, hard to cut cleanly with a mower
Most common in thin, dry, low-fertility turf

traits: Small daisy-like flower with a few simple white petals around a fuzzy yellow center
Compound leaves with toothed, pointed leaflets
Grows upright, often a foot or more tall in unmowed areas
Narrow, barbed black seeds that stick firmly to clothing, fur, and socks

look_alikes.difference: Spanish needles has white petals around a yellow center and barbed seeds sticking to clothes; Asiatic hawksbeard has small all-yellow flowers, no sticky seeds.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the flower (white petals with yellow center vs. all yellow) and the seed (barbed, sticky vs. fluffy like a dandelion).

copy.what_it_means: A common, disturbed-ground weed that shows up in beds, fence lines, and unmowed edges more than in a regularly cut lawn. It's mostly a nuisance from the barbed seeds sticking to clothes and pets rather than a threat to turf, and a technician looks at coverage and location before recommending an approach.
copy.fact: Its barbed black seeds are built to hitchhike on fur and fabric, which is why a walk through an overgrown lot can leave someone covered in them.
copy.blurb: A common disturbed-ground weed known for its barbed seeds that stick to clothes and pet fur.

tech_notes: Rarely a problem in regularly mowed turf; more common in beds, fence lines, and unmaintained edges. Per label if herbicide is used.

id_cues: Small daisy-like flower with a few white petals around a fuzzy yellow center
Compound leaves with toothed, pointed leaflets
Grows upright, taller in unmowed spots than most lawn weeds
Narrow black seeds with tiny barbs that catch on fabric and fur

traits: Tiny, fleshy, fern-like leaves on soft, translucent green stems
Forms low, spreading, moss-like clumps rather than a single upright plant
Grows in shaded mulch beds, planting beds, and cracks in driveways and hardscapes far more often than in open lawn
Flowers are tiny and inconspicuous, but forcefully eject pollen when ready — the source of the name

look_alikes.difference: Artilleryweed has tiny fern-like leaves on soft stems, growing in shaded mulch beds and cracks; spotted spurge has a maroon leaf spot, milky sap, sunnier spots.
look_alikes.next_photo: Wearing gloves, a close-up of the stem (soft and translucent vs. milky sap when broken) and where it grows (shaded bed vs. sunny thin turf); keep any sap away from your eyes.

copy.what_it_means: A fern-like, moss-textured weed that colonizes mulch beds, shaded corners, and cracks in driveways and walkways more than open lawn. It's a cosmetic bed weed for most homeowners, and a technician looks at coverage and location before recommending an approach.
copy.fact: It gets its name from forcefully ejecting pollen from its tiny flowers, almost like a tiny cannon firing — a real, if microscopic, spectacle.
copy.blurb: A fern-like, moss-textured weed that colonizes mulch beds and cracks in hardscapes.

tech_notes: More a bed/hardscape weed than a turf weed; check drain holes, ground cloth under mulch, and shaded cracks. Per label if herbicide is used.

id_cues: Tiny fern-like leaves on soft, nearly translucent green stems
Forms low, moss-like spreading clumps
Found in shaded mulch beds and cracks in hardscape more than open lawn
Stems are fragile and succulent, not woody

traits: Compound, fern-like leaves made of many tiny leaflets that fold up when touched
Round, fluffy, pink-to-lavender "powderpuff" flowers
Low, mat-forming, spreading growth in the common Florida native form; a shrubbier, thorned form also occurs
Tolerates some mowing and foot traffic once established

look_alikes.difference: Sensitive plant folds up when touched and has pink powderpuff flowers; chamberbitter doesn't react to touch, with tiny bead-like fruits under its leaf branches.
look_alikes.next_photo: Gently touch a leaflet, avoiding the prickly stems, and photograph the reaction (folds vs. no reaction), plus a wide shot of the flower if present.

copy.what_it_means: A native groundcover with fern-like leaves that fold when touched, sometimes kept on purpose as a low-mow lawn alternative and sometimes unwanted in a traditional turf lawn. A technician looks at customer preference along with coverage and turf type before recommending anything.
copy.fact: Its leaflets fold up within seconds of being touched or shaken, a real defense response rather than just a nickname.
copy.blurb: A touch-sensitive native groundcover — sometimes wanted, sometimes not, depending on the lawn.

tech_notes: Confirm whether the customer wants it removed or kept — it's a recognized turf alternative in some landscapes, not automatically a weed to eliminate. A shrubbier thorned Mimosa form also occurs; note thorns if present.

review.notes: Whether a given Mimosa specimen is the thornless native M. strigillosa or the thorned M. pudica is a per-photo call, not a fact this entry can settle generically — thorns indicate M. pudica, a thornless mat indicates M. strigillosa.

id_cues: Compound, fern-like leaves that fold shut within seconds of being touched
Round, fluffy, pink-to-lavender flower heads
Usually low and mat-forming; check for thorns on a shrubbier-looking plant
Can take some mowing and light foot traffic once established

traits: Soft, hairy, gray-green to whitish leaves forming a low rosette
Upright, felty flower stalk topped with small clusters of whitish-brown flowers, no showy petals
Low-growing, most noticeable in thin winter turf and disturbed soil
Whole plant has a soft, velvety or woolly feel

look_alikes.difference: Cudweed has soft, fuzzy gray-green leaves and small whitish-brown flowers, no showy petals; Asiatic hawksbeard has lobed leaves and small yellow flowers.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the flower color (whitish-brown vs. yellow) and whether the leaves feel fuzzy or smooth.

copy.what_it_means: A soft, fuzzy cool-season weed that moves into thin turf and newly disturbed soil over the winter and fades out once warm-season grass fills back in. A technician looks at how thin the turf is, the season, and coverage before recommending an approach.
copy.fact: Several look-alike cudweed species grow in Florida, some fuzzy gray-green and some glossier, and all of them serve as host plants for American painted lady butterfly caterpillars.
copy.blurb: A soft, fuzzy winter weed that moves into thin turf and fades as warm-season grass fills back in.

tech_notes: Cool-season annual; expect it to decline as turf resumes active growth in spring. Thin turf density is the underlying driver. Per label if herbicide is used.

id_cues: Soft, hairy, gray-green to whitish leaves in a low rosette
Upright, felty flower stalk with small whitish-brown flower clusters, no showy petals
Whole plant feels soft, velvety, or woolly to the touch
Shows up in thin winter turf and disturbed soil

traits: Thick, fleshy, succulent stems with lance-shaped leaves that sheath around the stem at the base
Showy flowers, often two or three blue petals plus a small whitish petal, opening for just a single day
Sprawling growth that roots at the nodes when stems touch soil
Can be confused with grass at a glance because of the parallel-veined leaf

look_alikes.difference: Dayflower has showy blue-and-white flowers on fleshy stems; doveweed has smaller purple flowers and leaves that mimic St. Augustinegrass, easy to overlook.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the flower (showy blue-and-white vs. small purple) and the leaf's resemblance to surrounding turf.

look_alikes.difference: Dayflower has fleshy, succulent stems and showy blue-and-white flowers; St. Augustinegrass has wide, blunt blades on stolons, no true flower visible when mowed.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the stem (fleshy and round vs. flat grass blade) and whether a flower is present.

copy.what_it_means: A succulent, grass-like weed that favors moist areas and can be mistaken for turf until its showy blue flower gives it away. A technician looks at weed type, turf type, season, and coverage, since like doveweed it can be harder to control in St. Augustine than most broadleaf weeds.
copy.fact: Each flower opens for only a single day before wilting, which is exactly where the name "dayflower" comes from.
copy.blurb: A succulent, grass-like weed with a showy blue flower that opens for just one day at a time.

tech_notes: Confirm against doveweed and St. Augustine — fleshy stem and the blue-and-white flower are the clearest tells. Stem fragments left behind after pulling can root again; per label if herbicide is used.

id_cues: Thick, fleshy, succulent stem, round rather than flat like a grass blade
Lance-shaped leaves that sheath around the stem at the base
Showy flower with two or three blue petals and a small whitish petal, open for a day
Roots wherever a stem node touches moist soil

traits: Glossy, dark green, lance-shaped leaves that closely resemble St. Augustinegrass blades
Thick, fleshy, succulent creeping stems (not true grass stolons)
Small purple, three-petaled flowers, easy to miss among the foliage
Grows unnoticed in a St. Augustine lawn until it forms a noticeably different-textured patch

look_alikes.difference: Doveweed's leaves are glossier, more succulent than St. Augustine's, with fleshy round stems, not true stolons, plus small purple flowers St. Augustine lacks.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up comparing leaf gloss and stem texture (fleshy and round vs. a true grass stolon) plus a wide shot checking for small purple flowers.

look_alikes.difference: Doveweed has small purple flowers and leaves that mimic St. Augustinegrass; dayflower has larger, showy blue-and-white flowers, easier to spot against turf.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the flower (small purple vs. showy blue-and-white).

copy.what_it_means: An aggressive summer weed that mimics St. Augustinegrass closely enough to grow unnoticed until it has already spread, and is genuinely hard to control once established. A technician evaluates the weed, turf type, season, and coverage to explain why this one needs a different approach than an ordinary broadleaf weed.
copy.fact: Its leaves are built to blend in — close enough to St. Augustinegrass that a patch can spread for weeks before anyone notices it isn't turf.
copy.blurb: A St. Augustine look-alike weed that spreads unnoticed and is genuinely hard to control once established.

tech_notes: Germinates when soil temps reach roughly 65-70F; a healthy, dense stand of turf is the best long-term defense. This one, along with torpedograss, is a legitimately difficult control case in St. Augustine — set expectations accordingly rather than promising quick results.

copy.what_it_means: A cool-season weed that shows up in thin turf and open ground over the winter, then dies back as the weather warms. A technician looks at how thin the turf is, the season and coverage before recommending an approach.
copy.fact: Henbit is in the mint family, so its stems are square rather than round, which is a quick way to tell it from look-alikes.
copy.blurb: A winter weed with square stems and purple-pink flowers that fades as the weather warms.

tech_notes: Winter annual that germinates in fall; the pre-emergent window is roughly October to early November in central and south Florida. Thin turf is the underlying driver. Per label if herbicide is used.
